docs: design for blob storage and in-memory databases

Two people have asked for many small databases kept in object storage, pulled
down per unit of work and pushed back, one of them without touching the local
filesystem at all.

The design records what the engine already supports, which turned out to be more
than expected. The storage layer makes no direct filesystem calls at all, so an
alternative backend is a matter of supplying one rather than carving out a path
for it. Only two places in the engine reach around the VFS.

It also records that four providers do not mean four SDKs. One SigV4
implementation reaches S3, Cloudflare R2, and Google Cloud Storage through its
S3-compatible API, which matters because the native Google path would need RS256
signing that std does not expose. Azure needs a second signer, not a second SDK.

Conditional writes are specified as part of the first phase rather than a later
addition, because the failure this architecture invites is two workers
overwriting each other with nothing reporting an error.

The double-buffering question is answered with a borrow-for-reads,
copy-on-write scheme, and with the sequencing to ship copying first and measure
before touching the buffer pool.

Replication's outstanding object-storage phase is folded into this, since it
needs the same interface for a different reason.

docs: put serialization before signing in the blob design

The first draft led with implementing SigV4 and SharedKey in the engine. That was
the wrong starting point, and the reason is not effort.

Both people who asked for this have applications, and those applications already
have a cloud SDK, credentials, and a retry policy somebody has opinions about. An
engine that implements SigV4 reimplements, worse, what the caller already has, and
takes custody of long-lived cloud credentials to do it. A database that holds
credentials is a different proposition from one that does not, and that is not a
trade to make in order to save the caller four lines.

The design is now three layers. Serialization over readers and writers needs no
network at all and is the whole of what was asked for. Transfer against a
caller-supplied presigned URL needs no provider-specific code, because every
provider's presigned URL is just a URL, and it streams, so a large database does
not have to exist twice in memory. Native signers are left for the one case with
no application in the loop, which is replication shipping to a bucket, and which
nobody has asked for yet.

storage: serialize a database to bytes and back

Database.serialize hands back the whole database as a block of bytes, and
Database.deserialize opens one from them. That is the piece people need to keep
many small databases in object storage: pull the blob, open it, change it, push
it back.

It is cheap because a database here is one file, so serialising it is reading
that file. The same request is hard for engines that spread a database over a
catalog, indexes, and a log, because they have to invent a container format and
keep it in step with themselves. This is the reason the single-file format was
worth having.

The application does its own uploading and downloading, with the client,
credentials, and retry policy it already has. An engine that spoke to S3 itself
would be reimplementing, worse, what the caller already has, and taking custody
of cloud credentials to do it.

Pending writes are folded in first, so the bytes need no log beside them, and
serialising is refused while a transaction is open for the same reason backup is:
a copy taken while writes land underneath it is torn in ways nothing downstream
would notice until it was needed. The flushing step is now shared with backup
rather than duplicated, since a second copy would drift.

Deserialize checks the bytes look like a database before writing them anywhere.
Without that, an empty or truncated download would be written out, opened, and
silently turned into a brand new empty database, because opening a zero-length
file is how a database gets created. That would report success and lose
everything.

The file it materialises is owned by the returned handle and removed when it
closes, so a workflow that runs per request leaves nothing behind. That file goes
away entirely once databases can live in memory.

feat(api): expose serialize and deserialize through the C API

lattice_serialize hands back an owned buffer, released with lattice_free_bytes,
and lattice_deserialize opens a database from one. The bytes are copied, so a
caller may free them as soon as deserialize returns rather than having to keep
them alive for the life of the database.

Handle adoption is factored out of the open path rather than written twice, since
both entry points have to register the handle and both have to close the database
if registration fails.

feat(bindings): serialize and deserialize in Python, TypeScript, and Go

Database.serialize returns the database as bytes in every language, and each
gets a deserialize that opens one from bytes: a package-level function in Python
and TypeScript, latticedb.Deserialize in Go.

All three copy the bytes out of native memory before releasing the buffer the
engine handed them, so what the caller holds does not depend on memory that has
already been freed. Deserialize copies the other way too, so callers may reuse or
discard their slice as soon as it returns.

The documentation on each shows the workflow the feature exists for, including
the conditional write. Two workers that read the same object, change it, and
write it back will otherwise silently overwrite each other, with nothing
reporting an error, and that is worth putting in front of people rather than
leaving them to discover it.

docs: cover keeping many small databases in object storage

The backup guide covered protecting one database and said nothing about the other
shape of the problem, which comes up just as often: many small databases, one per
case or tenant or document, living in a bucket and pulled down when needed.

The new section shows the round trip, explains why it is cheap here, and says
plainly that the engine does no networking on purpose. An application already has
a storage client, credentials, and a retry policy somebody chose; a database that
reimplemented those would do a worse job of something the caller already has, and
would have to hold their cloud credentials to do it.

It also covers the failure this pattern invites, which is not in the database:
two workers overwriting each other with nothing reporting an error. The
conditional write is shown in every example rather than mentioned as an aside.

docs: correct the in-memory write-ahead log recommendation

The design said an in-memory database should default to running without a log,
reasoning that a process holding the only copy loses everything when it dies, so
the log is pure cost.

Testing it says otherwise. With the log off, beginTransaction returns
TransactionsNotEnabled: there are no explicit transactions at all, so no
multi-statement atomicity and no rollback. That is a much larger hole than the
allocations it saves, and it would make in-memory databases quietly less capable
than file-backed ones in a way nobody would expect.

The log stays on, as a second file in the same memory VFS, bounded by automatic
checkpointing at a few megabytes.

docs: write up phase 2, in-memory databases

Records what the discussion settled. The memory backend is asked for with a
:memory: path rather than an option, because every binding already passes a path
string through and an option would mean a new C struct version and four binding
changes for the same capability. Storage is chunked from the start, because a
growing contiguous buffer is reallocated as it grows and that invalidates every
borrow handed out beforehand.

It also corrects the cost of double buffering, which an earlier draft had wrong.
The buffer pool is fixed size and allocated eagerly, so peak memory is the
database plus the pool rather than twice the database. That turns the problem
around: the waste is not large databases but small ones, where a five megabyte
database allocates forty megabytes of frames it can never fill. Capping the
in-memory pool at the database size plus headroom is strictly better there and a
no-op everywhere else.

Pool-level borrowing moves to last rather than first. It targets the caching copy,
which is the one part of the pool that stops mattering in memory and whose size
the sizing rule now bounds, and it would put a new state into the structure that
pinning, latching, and dirty tracking all run through.

storage: run a database entirely in memory

Opening ":memory:" gives a database with no files behind it, and deserialize now
lands there directly rather than writing bytes to a temporary file first. That
was the thing somebody keeping small databases in object storage asked for: pull
a blob, work on it, hand the bytes back, and never touch the local disk.

The storage layer already reached disk only through the Vfs interface, so this is
a new backend rather than a new path through the engine. A database owns its
backend by value, because the interface is a fat pointer and a caller-supplied
one would have to outlive the database, which is a lifetime rule nobody should
have to think about.

":memory:" is a path rather than an option because every binding already passes a
path string straight through. An option would have meant another versioned C
struct and four bindings changed for the same capability.

Memory files are stored as page-sized chunks rather than one growing buffer. The
reason is not allocation churn: a contiguous buffer is reallocated as it grows,
and that moves every byte, so anything holding a borrowed slice would be left
pointing at freed memory. Chunks are what make lending bytes possible at all, and
retrofitting them later would mean doing it under pressure.

Two things had to change to keep this honest. Backup wrote its temporary file
through the database's own filesystem, which for an in-memory database meant
writing the backup into memory and then renaming a file that was never created;
the destination is a real path by definition and now uses a real filesystem.
And deleting a stale log during recovery went straight to the filesystem, which
would have tried to remove an actual file called ":memory:-wal".

The buffer pool is capped at the size of an in-memory database plus a floor. A
pool larger than the database can never fill its extra frames, so capping it is
strictly better there and a no-op for anything bigger than the budget. Measured
on a hundred-kilobyte database, overhead drops from 16 MB to 1 MB. The floor
exists because a pool with nowhere to put the next page fails the query rather
than slowing it down.

Locks always succeed in memory, deliberately: a lock keeps a second process off a
database, and no other process can reach memory this one owns.

storage: opening ":memory:" implies creating it

Opening an in-memory database without asking to create it failed with
FileNotFound, which is technically true and useless: there is never a previous
in-memory database lying around to find, so requiring create would be a
formality every caller has to remember and every binding has to document.

This is what makes the path approach actually free. `lattice exec :memory:`,
`latticedb.Database(":memory:")`, `new Database(':memory:')`, and
`latticedb.Open(":memory:", OpenOptions{})` now all work with no binding changes
at all, which was the whole argument for choosing a path over an option.

Verified through the command line and all three bindings: a write, a read, a
serialize, and nothing appearing on disk in any of them.

Where deserialize has already seeded the backend, the file is present and create
opens it rather than replacing it.

storage: let deserialize borrow the caller's bytes

Copying a blob into the memory backend means the database exists twice while it
loads. Passing borrow_bytes points the backend at the caller's buffer instead,
and each page becomes a copy of its own the first time something writes to it.
A workload that opens a case, reads it, and changes a little of it therefore
holds one copy of nearly all of it rather than two.

This is what the chunked layout was for. Chunks are now either owned or borrowed,
and writing is what converts one, which is copy-on-write at page granularity.

The bytes have to outlive the database, so it is off by default and not every
language can offer it. Go may not let C retain a pointer into its heap at all,
and pinning a Java array for the life of a database would hold up the collector
for exactly as long. Those bindings copy, which is a language rule rather than
anything about how carefully they are written.

Both properties are asserted rather than assumed: that borrowing allocates less
than copying, and that the caller's buffer comes back byte for byte unchanged
after forty writes. A write that reached through to the caller's memory would
make their idea of what they hold quietly stop being true, which is the kind of
thing that surfaces a long way from its cause.

byteCount now reports only what the filesystem allocated for itself, since
borrowed bytes are somebody else's memory and counting them would misreport what
an in-memory database costs.

feat(bindings): let Python and TypeScript deserialize without copying

Passing copy=False points the database at the caller's buffer rather than
duplicating it, so a freshly loaded database costs about half what it did. Each
page becomes a copy of its own the first time it is written, and the caller's
bytes are never modified.

Borrowing is a separate C entry point rather than a field on the options struct.
It carries an obligation about how long the bytes have to live, and a bool buried
in a struct is too quiet a place to put one; lattice_deserialize_borrowed puts it
where somebody reading the call will see it.

Each binding holds a reference to the buffer on the wrapper object, so the
lifetime rule is satisfied without asking callers to think about it.

Go and Java are not offered this, which is a language rule rather than an
oversight. Go's own documentation says C code may not keep a copy of a Go pointer
after the call returns, and pinning a Java array for the life of a database would
hold up the collector for exactly that long.

The Python path uses ctypes.cast rather than from_buffer_copy. The first version
of this used from_buffer_copy on both branches, which copied on the path whose
entire purpose is not copying, and still passed a test that only checked the
rows came back.

docs: cover in-memory databases and borrowed loads

The backup guide and the command reference now cover opening ":memory:", and the
guide explains loading a blob without a second copy of it in memory.

It also says why Go and Java do not offer borrowing, because "this binding has
fewer options" reads like an oversight unless the reason is written down: their
rules forbid holding a pointer into managed memory for the lifetime of a
database, however carefully the binding is written.

storage: set the in-memory pool floor from a measurement

The floor was 256 frames, chosen by guessing, and it decided how much memory a
small in-memory database costs. Guessing it trades memory against query failures,
and neither side of that trade should be a hunch.

Measured instead: pools from four frames upward were run against a fifteen-hundred
node graph with edges and a text index, through a deep variable-length traversal,
a filtered scan, a full-text search, and a bulk write. Four frames completed all
of it. The engine does not hold many pages pinned at once.

The floor is now sixty-four, sixteen times the observed requirement, because the
measurement was single threaded and concurrent readers each pin pages of their
own. A hundred-kilobyte in-memory database drops from 1128 KB to 360 KB, against
16484 KB for the same database backed by a file.

A first attempt measured this by instrumenting the pin counter and reported three
hundred thousand simultaneous pins on a two-thousand node database, which is
impossible: there was a decrement path the instrumentation missed. Measuring the
smallest pool that completes the work needed no instrumentation and could not
drift. Both the number and that mistake are recorded in the design, because the
wrong approach looked more rigorous than the right one.

The measurement is pinned as a test running against an eight-frame pool, so a
change that starts holding many more pages fails there with an obvious cause
rather than as a mysterious BufferPoolFull in somebody's small database.

docs: say what the full-text search operator actually does

Two things about @@ surprise people, and one of them was demonstrated by the
documentation itself.

Storing a string in a property does not index it. Text has to be handed to the
index on purpose, and a node whose property was never indexed simply never
matches, with nothing to say why.

The property name on the left of @@ is not used at all. The index holds one
document per node rather than one per property, so `d.content @@ "..."` asks
whether the node's indexed text matches, not whether its content property does.
`d.title`, `d.content`, and a misspelled property name all behave identically:
a node matches on text that has nothing to do with the property named, and a
typo in that name is never reported.

The guide's own example created a node with a title property, indexed a sentence
unrelated to it, and then searched `d.content`, which was not a property of
anything. That is exactly the confusion being documented.

storage: give in-memory databases a small fixed pool, and say why

The sizing rule read as the smaller of the configured budget and the database
plus a floor. That was not what it did. At the point it runs, a freshly created
database is a single page, so the formula always returned the floor while looking
as though it scaled with the data — and a deserialized database, whose page count
is real at open, got a different answer for no articulable reason.

Behaviour is unchanged, because the accidental answer turns out to be the right
one. The pool exists to keep pages off a disk, and a miss against memory is a copy
from one part of RAM to another. Measured on a fourteen megabyte in-memory
database, twelve full scans took 9.2 seconds against a 256 KB pool and 9.9 against
a 32 MB one: a hundred and twenty times the memory bought nothing.

So the code now says a small fixed pool and explains that, rather than computing
the same number through an expression that implies otherwise.

The same measurement closes pool-level borrowing. Total overhead across sizes runs
2.62x at a hundred nodes down to 1.01x at ten thousand, with the pool a constant
256 KB throughout. Borrowing pages could save at most that, against adding "this
frame might not own its bytes" to the structure every read and write goes through.
The remaining overhead at small sizes is the write-ahead log rather than
duplication, which is why the ratio falls as the database grows instead of rising.

fix(query): sort by an aggregate after computing it, not before

ORDER BY, SKIP, and LIMIT were planned underneath the projection, so a query that
aggregated sorted its raw matches and then regrouped them, throwing the ordering
away. This returned rows in an order nobody asked for, with no error and nothing
downstream able to tell.

    MATCH (a:Author)-[:WROTE]->(p:Paper)
    RETURN a.name AS name, count(p) AS papers ORDER BY papers DESC

    before: two(2), one(1), three(3)
    after:  three(3), two(2), one(1)

Top-N by count is one of the most common analytical queries there is, so this was
producing plausible wrong answers in a very ordinary shape.

Where the clauses belong depends on the projection. Without aggregation they stay
underneath, because sorting by n.name needs the n that projection is about to
discard. With aggregation they go on top, and sorting reads the output column
rather than evaluating: the expression is count(p), and rows reaching the sort
have already been grouped, so there is no p left to count. SortItem gains an
optional slot for that.

LIMIT and SKIP move with it, which is what makes top-N mean the top rather than
an arbitrary subset of the matches.

Naming a column the projection does not produce is now refused. Sorting by
something that is not there cannot be done, and answering with rows in some
arbitrary order is how this went unnoticed in the first place.

Non-aggregate ordering is unchanged, and the tests cover ascending as well as
descending so a sort that happens to leave things alone cannot pass both.

docs: design per-property full-text search

The @@ operator looks like it searches a property and does not. The index holds
one document per node, so the property name is read by the planner and thrown
away: d.title, d.content, and a misspelled name all behave identically, and a node
matches on text that has nothing to do with the property named.

The design follows the explicit property index rather than inventing anything. It
already has a catalog of declared definitions, automatic maintenance on every
write, and one B-tree serving every definition by prefixing keys with the scope
and property symbol ids. Full-text search can use all three, which means no new
trees in the file header.

One node with several indexed properties becomes several documents rather than
one. Merging them would make a title part of a long document, so a term in the
title would score as though it were buried in a page of body text. Keeping them
apart compares titles against titles, and happens to be simpler: within one index
a node appears once, so the document identifier stays the node id.

Two decisions are recorded as taken. ftsIndexDocument is removed rather than kept
alongside, so there is one concept instead of two. And searching a property with
no declared index is an error naming the missing index rather than an empty
result, because an empty result is indistinguishable from nothing matching, which
is exactly how the current behaviour goes unnoticed.

The first of those has a cost worth stating plainly: text that was indexed but is
not stored in a property cannot be rebuilt, because the database never held it
anywhere else. Old index entries are therefore left inert rather than cleared on
open, since deleting them during an upgrade would destroy the only copy.

fix(fts): stop scoring against freed memory and lost statistics

Two bugs, found while preparing per-property indexes, which would otherwise have
been inherited once per index instead of once.

FtsIndex.init built a DocLengthStore as a local, copied it into the returned
struct, and handed the scorer the address of the local, which died when the
constructor returned. Every BM25 score was computed by reading freed stack memory.

A workaround at one call site rebuilt the scorer with the correct address after
indexing a document, which is exactly why this stayed hidden: indexing and then
searching worked, and searching without indexing first did not. The second case is
most sessions in production.

The scorer now holds no reference at all and takes the statistics it needs as an
argument. That removes the possibility rather than repairing the one instance, and
it makes the lifetime visible at every call site.

Underneath that, corpus statistics were never written down. Document lengths went
to a tree; the document count and average length that BM25 needs to interpret them
were kept in memory, initialised to zero, and lost on close. Scores therefore
changed on every restart — on one test corpus a document moved 65 per cent, and
with an average length of zero the length normalisation collapses entirely, so a
term in a title stops outranking the same term buried in a page of text.

Statistics are now stored under a key that cannot collide with a document id,
since document keys are always eight bytes and this one is six.

Both are covered by tests that compare scores across a close and reopen, and that
check a short document still outranks a long one. The first fails against a build
where the statistics are not loaded back.

The book explained the query language across fourteen pages, and how the engine
works internally across another fourteen, with nothing in between about running

an API reference, some only in the release notes that introduced them.

Three pages, aimed at somebody who has it working and now has to decide how to
configure it.

actually deciding: what is permanent from creation, which features exist, memory,
safety, and durability. It says which choices cannot be changed later without

fts: add a catalog of declared full-text indexes

First stage of making @@ mean what it reads like. A declared index says that a
named property on a named label holds text worth searching, which is the thing
the operator has always implied and never checked.

Definitions share the tree that already holds property index definitions. Its
keys are [kind, scope_id, property_id], and the leading byte already separates
nodes from edges, so full-text definitions need only their own values of it:
3 and 4, continuing where property indexes stop at 1 and 2. No new tree, no new
slot in the file header, and nothing already stored reads differently.

Nothing uses this yet. It carries create, drop, has, and an iterator, plus the
lookup that @@ will ask, and the prefix that will scope stored terms to one index
so a term indexed for a title cannot be found when searching a body.

The tests cover what would break quietly: node and edge definitions not colliding,
neither being mistakable for a property index definition in the same tree, and
keys ordering by kind so an iterator sees one kind at a time.

in its name, so scanning the sidebar for it found nothing, and two readers in a

The lesson worth keeping: checking that documentation exists is not the same as

docs: reject multi-property full-text indexes, and say why

An earlier note suggested letting one index cover several properties, on the
grounds that single-property would then be the one-element case. That is true of
the storage and false of the syntax, which is the half that matters.

If an index merges title and body, then `d.title @@ "x"` matches documents whose
body contains the term. The property name is lying again, which is the exact bug
this design exists to remove. Reusing property access requires one property per
index; naming the index instead needs syntax Cypher does not have and a second
namespace to keep.

The migration is also better than it first looked. Somebody searching several
fields stores the combined text in a property and indexes that, which gives the
same single document and the same merged score, with the searchable text visible
in the database rather than hidden inside an index. That visibility is precisely
what the old API lacked and why it cannot be migrated automatically.

Merged ranking across separately indexed properties is recorded as the real
remaining gap, and as a syntax question rather than a storage one.

fix(query): make @@ mean the same thing wherever it appears

The planner recognises a full-text match only when it is the whole WHERE clause.
Anywhere else, inside AND or OR, the expression fell through to a filter that did
a case-insensitive substring test against the property's raw text: no index, no
stemming, no scoring, and a full scan.

So the same predicate searched different data depending on where it sat, and the
two disagreed about which documents matched. With text indexed as
'ciabatta focaccia' on a node whose title property reads 'sourdough':

    WHERE d.title @@ 'ciabatta'                   -> 1 row
    WHERE d.title @@ 'ciabatta' OR d.body @@ 'zz' -> 0 rows
    WHERE d.title @@ 'sourdough'                  -> 0 rows
    WHERE d.title @@ 'sourdough' OR d.body @@ 'zz'-> 1 row

Exactly inverted. Adding an unrelated OR beside a correct query silently turned
it into an incorrect one, with nothing to indicate anything had changed.

A full-text match now asks the index wherever it appears. Asking one node at a
time is slower than scanning the index once, which is why the planner still
prefers a scan when it can build one, and why a disjunction of scans is the next
piece of work. A filter that agrees with the scan is worth more than a fast filter
that disagrees with it.

One case keeps its old meaning, and the distinction is now principled rather than
positional. `"some text" @@ "query"` has no node and no indexed document behind
it, so it asks the self-contained question of whether that text contains those
terms. The index is consulted when there is a document to consult.

fts: give each full-text index its own space in the shared trees

The dictionary, document lengths, and reverse index are one tree each, shared by
every index that will be declared. Without something separating them, a term
indexed for one property would be found when searching another, which is the
behaviour per-property indexes exist to replace.

Every key now carries a four-byte prefix naming the index it belongs to. That
happens inside a view wrapping the tree rather than at each place a key is built,
of which there are a dozen across three files. Missing one of those would not fail
to compile: it would write an entry the matching read could never find, or read
another index's. One place to get right is worth more than twelve places to
remember.

The stores hold that view instead of the tree, and not one line of their
key-building code changed. FtsIndex.initScoped takes an optional scope, and
passing null gives the index that exists today, so both schemes work while the old
one is still in use.

Two bugs were made and fixed while writing this, both worth recording because they
are the same bug.

Building the prefixed bounds in local buffers and handing slices to the tree's
iterator leaves it comparing against freed stack, since it keeps the end key and
checks it on every step. That is exactly what the scorer was doing with its
document store earlier today. It appeared to work, because the bytes are usually
still there, and surfaced only when a refactor moved the stack: an index started
returning its neighbour's entries. The iterator now owns its bounds. Then the
dictionary's own iterator reintroduced it by copying the inner iterator out of a
local, so that one owns the scoped iterator rather than a copy of it.

The prefix arithmetic has its own trap. A prefix ending in 0xff has to carry into
the byte before it, or the range end wraps below the start and the index looks
empty. That is a function with its cases tested, rather than arithmetic written
twice.

fix(index): stop the property index walking definitions off a dead stack

BTree.range uses the start key while it descends and then keeps the end key,
comparing every entry against it for as long as the iterator lives. A function
that builds both bounds in locals and returns the iterator is therefore handing
back a pointer into a stack frame it just left.

definitionIterator did exactly that, and the property index walks its definitions
through it on the write path: indexNode, removeNode, indexEdge, removeEdge, and
the rebuild after recovery all go through this. The failure it produces is not a
crash. It reads whatever the next call happened to leave on that stack, so the
walk either ends early or never starts, and which of those happens depends on the
shape of the caller's frame.

That is why it has been sitting here working. Nothing about it is stable, though,
and a change to an unrelated caller could have turned it into indexes that quietly
stop being maintained.

It was found from the other end. The full-text catalog was given the same shape,
copied from here, and its walk came back empty, so no write ever updated a
declared index. Proving it took three attempts, and the middle one is the reason
this is worth writing down: a test calling the old shape in isolation passed, and
a probe that built both the old and the fixed iterator inside the failing function
saw both of them work. The probe's own locals had moved the frame enough for the
freed bytes to survive. Only the write path using the old shape alone failed
again. Measuring it changed it.

The iterator now owns its bounds, so the lifetime is the caller's to see. The
other sixteen callers of range are fine: they either pass no end bound or keep the
iterator in the function that built it.

fts: populate declared indexes and keep them current

Declaring an index reads the property off every entity that already carries the
label and indexes it, following what createNodePropertyIndex does for the same
reason: an index that only covers what arrives after it is declared is not much of
an index.

After that the write path maintains it. Create, update, and delete all funnel
through two functions, one for nodes and one for edges, where an empty old state
means a create and an empty new state means a delete. Eight call sites reach them,
and having one place decide what a change means beats eight places each deciding
it again.

Text that did not change is left alone. Without that, writing any property on an
entity would reindex its longest indexed string, and the cost of an unrelated
write would scale with how much text the entity happens to carry.

Only string properties are indexed. A number or a list is not text, and turning
one into some rendering of itself so a search for 42 could match an integer is a
different feature with different rules; doing half of it silently would make
results hard to explain.

Recovery rebuilds. Redo replays into the stores directly rather than through the
write path, so nothing maintains the indexes while it runs, exactly as the
property indexes already have to handle. The rebuild clears by scope rather than
walking documents, because an entity the redo deleted is no longer there to walk
and its terms would otherwise stay behind and keep matching. That needs a
delete-everything-under-this-prefix, which is a batched collect-then-delete: the
tree's iterator pins a leaf and holds a slot in it, so deleting while iterating is
not safe, and a fixed batch keeps the memory flat rather than proportional to what
is often the largest structure in the database.

The posting pages of a cleared index stay allocated. Nothing points at them once
the dictionary entries naming them are gone, so it is wasted space rather than
wrong data, and reclaiming it needs page reuse the store does not have yet.

ftsSearchIndex searches one declaration and scores against that index's own
corpus, so a term common in titles and rare in bodies is judged separately in
each. It reports a missing index rather than an empty result, because a typo in a
property name and a query that found nothing are different situations and should
not look identical.

Declaring is refused when full-text search is disabled, since removing a document
needs the reverse index to say which terms it wrote and where. An index that could
not be maintained would go stale on its first update, which is worse than saying
no here.

fts: make @@ search the index declared for the property it names

Until now the property in `d.title @@ "bread"` selected nothing. There was one
index holding one document per node, so every property name searched the same
text and `d.title` and `d.body` returned identical answers. The property name was
decoration.

It now resolves to a declared index. The label comes from the pattern the variable
was written in, which is where property index planning already takes it from, and
the label and property together name exactly one index.

Two things that used to return no rows are now errors, because no rows is
indistinguishable from a search that found nothing, and that is how a mistyped
property name goes unnoticed for a long time:

    MATCH (d:Doc) WHERE d.title @@ 'sourdough' RETURN d.title
      No full-text index is declared for Doc.title. Declare one before searching it.

    MATCH (d) WHERE d.title @@ 'sourdough' RETURN d.title
      `d.title @@ ...` needs a label to say which full-text index it means.
      Write it in the pattern, as in (d:Label).

The second one refuses to guess. Two labels can each declare an index on `title`,
so an unlabelled pattern does not say which is meant, and picking one would make
the answer depend on what else happens to be declared. A WITH clears the labels
for the same reason: what comes through it is an alias, not a node written with a
label.

Saying that at all needed a change beyond this feature. Every planning failure
reached the user as "could not create execution plan", which is true of all of
them and useful for none, so the planner now carries a specific explanation when
it has one.

A search inside an open transaction reads that transaction's own uncommitted
writes. A node whose text changed is scored from the pending text and one whose
text stopped matching drops out, which is the same treatment the unscoped search
already gave uncommitted documents.

The tests migrated the way users will have to. They indexed text that was stored
in no property at all — ftsIndexDocument with one string while the query asked
about `a.text`, which was not a property on those nodes — and that is exactly the
case the design says cannot be rebuilt automatically. It was sitting in our own
suite. The fix is to put the text in the property and declare an index over it.

Two tests written earlier this week lost their premise rather than their point.
They deliberately made the indexed text share no words with the property text, to
catch a filter path that read the wrong data. Per-property indexes make that
impossible to construct, so they now assert the invariant that survives: a term in
`body` is not found by a search of `title`, in either syntactic position.

fix(query): stop @@ silently returning the first hundred matches

The planner passed 100 as the result limit for a full-text index scan, hardcoded,
with a comment calling it the default. A query that named no limit got one anyway:

    MATCH (d:Doc) WHERE d.title @@ 'loaf' RETURN d.title      100 rows
    MATCH (d:Doc) WHERE d.title @@ 'loaf' OR ... RETURN ...   5000 rows

Same predicate, same data, no LIMIT written anywhere. The row filter used its own
much larger bound, so moving a predicate into an OR changed how many rows came
back. Counting over a common term would have answered 100 for as long as anyone
cared to ask.

This is the same shape as the bug fixed last week, where `@@` meant one thing at
the top of a WHERE clause and another inside a boolean expression. That one was
about which data was read. This one is about how much of it was returned, and it
has been here since `@@` was first wired into the planner.

Both paths now share one bound, and that bound is no bound: a predicate with no
LIMIT beside it means every matching row. An explicit LIMIT still applies, since
it is planned separately.

It was found while benchmarking the row filter against the index scan, from the
two disagreeing on how many rows they returned. The benchmark was measuring
something else and would have reported a comfortable-looking ratio between two
queries that were not answering the same question.

Removing the cap immediately panicked on integer overflow, because the search
widens the caller's limit to leave room for filtering and nothing had ever passed
a large one. Eleven multiplications and two additions across the full-text search
had the same latency; all of them saturate now.

fts: expose declaring an index through the C API and Go

Required rather than planned. The Go conformance suite searches `d.text @@
"graph"`, which now needs an index declared for Document.text, and nothing
outside Zig could declare one. CI failed on exactly that.

The suite migrated the way its users will have to. It indexed text held in no
property at all, then queried a property that did not exist on those nodes, which
is the case the design says cannot be rebuilt automatically. It now stores the
text and declares an index over it, and keeps the old per-node indexing beside it
so the direct FTSSearch assertion still has something to read until that API goes
away.

The conformance suite was not in the local validation loop, which is why this
reached CI. It is now.

fts: plan a disjunction of @@ as one union of index scans

Only a bare `@@` became an index scan. Put the same predicate inside an OR and
the whole condition fell to the row filter, which searched an index once per
candidate row. For a term most documents contain, that is quadratic:

    nodes    scan     OR     ratio
      200   4.8ms   11ms      3.3x
     1000    16ms  137ms      8.3x
     5000   113ms  3.3s      29.7x

A disjunction of `@@` predicates on one variable is now a single operator that
reads each declared index once and unions the results. The same measurement after:

    nodes    scan     OR     ratio
      200   4.8ms  4.8ms      1.0x
     1000    24ms   24ms      1.0x
     5000   130ms  133ms      1.0x

A document found by more than one search takes its best score rather than a sum.
Either side matching is enough for the row to be returned, and matching both is
not evidence of matching either one better; adding the scores would rank a
document that matched two properties weakly above one that matched a single
property strongly.

The union only applies when every disjunct is an `@@` on the same variable.
`d.title @@ 'x' OR d.name = 'y'` is not a union of index scans and keeps the row
filter, which still answers it correctly. Sixteen disjuncts is the cap, well past
anything written by hand, and it keeps the collected searches in a fixed array
rather than an allocation the operator would have to outlive.

The two constructors became one taking a list of searches, so a single predicate
is a list of one and there is one path through the operator rather than two.

The merged results belong to the operator's own allocator, not the database's.
Each search's results are freed as that search finishes; only the union survives,
and three cleanup paths had to stop freeing it through the wrong allocator.

fts!: remove the unscoped index and scope every search to a declaration

BREAKING CHANGE: ftsIndexDocument and its equivalents in every binding are gone,
and every search now names the label and property whose index answers it.

What went away is a single index holding one document per node. Text was handed
to it directly, so it lived nowhere the database could show you, and every
property name searched the same text: `d.title @@ "x"` and `d.body @@ "x"` were
the same query, and so was `d.nonexistent @@ "x"`.

An index now covers one label and one property. Declaring it reads that property
from every node already carrying the label, so an existing database becomes
searchable the moment you declare, without rewriting data. Writes maintain it
from then on, the way a property index is maintained.

Text that was indexed and stored in no property cannot be migrated
automatically, because the database never held it anywhere else. That case is
not hypothetical: it was in our own integration tests, the Go conformance suite,
and the quipu regression test, all three of which assembled a searchable string
out of several fields. Each of them now stores the assembled text in a property
and declares an index over it, which is exactly what the migration guide asks of
users.

Two bugs surfaced while scoping fuzzy search, both shipped by the scoped-storage
commit, both invisible until now for the same reason: nothing had ever run a
scoped dictionary walk. Fuzzy and prefix search were its only callers and both
ran against the unscoped index.

Dictionary.iterate built an owning iterator as a local and returned it by value.
Copying the struct moved the bound buffers while the inner iterator went on
comparing against the copy left behind. That is the fourth instance of this bug
in this work, and the pattern is the fault: an iterator that owns its bounds
cannot be returned by value at all. It writes into caller storage now, like the
other three.

Worse, the scoped iterator returned terms with the four-byte scope prefix still
attached. Exact lookup did not care, because keys are prefixed on the way in too.
Fuzzy matching measures edit distance against the term text, so every term sat
four edits further away than it was and no typo ever matched. ScopedTree.callerKey
existed to strip it; the iterator never called it.

Separately, ftsSearchFuzzyInTxn accepted max_distance and min_term_length,
discarded both, and ran an exact search. Fuzzy search inside a transaction has
never been fuzzy. Both forms go through the real matcher now. Uncommitted text is
still matched by term presence rather than edit distance, which is a real limit
and is documented rather than hidden.

The standalone FtsSearch operator went too: 131 lines with no callers, superseded
by FtsSearchWithInput and still compiling only because nothing forced the issue.

The four C search entry points each carried their own copy of the result-handle
bookkeeping. They share one function now, so an allocation failure unwinds the
same way in all of them.

docs: teach per-property full-text search, and how to migrate to it

The Cypher chapter had a section called "Two things that surprise people". Both
surprises were the behaviour this release removes: that storing a string did not
index it, and that the property name on the left of `@@` was decorative. Neither
is true now, so the section is gone and the chapter says what the operator does
instead.

A migration guide leads with the case that cannot be automated. If the text you
indexed is already in a property, declaring an index over it is the whole job and
your existing rows are picked up. If you assembled a searchable string out of
several fields, the database never held it and cannot rebuild it: you store the
assembled text in a property and backfill it, because only you know how it was
built.

That case looked like a corner until this work went looking for it. It turned up
in our integration tests, the Go conformance suite, and the quipu regression
test, so the guide treats it as the common one rather than a footnote.

Every example across the book, the top-level README, and the four binding READMEs
now declares an index and searches it by label and property. The performance page
had it backwards as well: it advised indexing only the text you search, on the
grounds that indexing wastes memory, when the cost that matters is that every
declared index is maintained on every write touching its property.

fts: make @@ reach relationship indexes

Stage 3 built storage and maintenance for edge full-text indexes because it fell
almost free out of the node work, and stage 4 then built query resolution for
nodes only, because that is what `@@` had always been. The design said edges were
in "unless it falls out for free", and half of it did. So the storage shipped and
nothing could query it.

Nothing structural was in the way. Edge variables already get slots, SlotValue
already answers asEdgeId, and edge_bindings already recorded the type. What was
node-only was the resolution, the operator, and the row filter.

    MATCH (a:Person)-[x:REVIEWED]->(p:Paper)
    WHERE x.note @@ "thorough"
    RETURN p.title

Three things needed deciding rather than copying.

A pattern may name several types. `-[r:A|B]->` kept only types[0], which was
enough for the DELETE metadata it was collected for and not enough here. Every
type is recorded now and tried in turn, the way a multi-label node resolves.

A slot holds a node or an edge, and which one decides where the document id comes
from. Reading an edge slot as a node id returns null rather than failing, so an
edge search would have matched nothing at all and looked like an empty index.

A disjunction cannot mix them. `d.title @@ "x" OR r.note @@ "x"` is not a union of
index scans, because one operator filters one slot. The planner declines to fuse
those and the row filter answers it correctly instead.

The overlay merge now covers edges, so a search inside a transaction sees edge
text that transaction has written and not yet committed. Without it the two kinds
would have behaved differently in the one place a reader is entitled to see its
own writes.

Declaring an edge index existed only in Zig, which would have left the feature
unreachable from every binding even with the query side fixed. That was found by
writing `db.create_edge_fts_index(...)` into the book and then checking whether it
existed. It did not. It now goes through the C API and all four bindings.

Tests drive it end to end through Cypher from Python, TypeScript, Go, and Java,
plus the Zig integration tests covering the scan path, the row filter inside an
OR, the missing-type error, and uncommitted edge writes.

docs: cover relationship indexes in the migration guide

The guide was written before `@@` could reach relationship indexes and described
only nodes, which made it wrong by omission the moment that landed.

Relationship text is new rather than changed, so there is nothing to migrate. The
guide says that plainly instead of leaving readers to work out whether they have
missed a step, and mentions the one workaround worth undoing: copying relationship
text onto an endpoint because there was no way to search it where it lived.

perf(query): make full-text search an access path instead of a filter

A `@@` predicate read the index to find out which documents matched, then
scanned every node carrying the label and kept the ones the index had named.
Answering a one-document query cost the whole corpus. At eight thousand
documents that was 72ms for work the index had already done in 31us.

Three changes, measured at eight thousand documents:

                        before      after
    @@ 'rare'            72ms       105us
    @@ 'rare' AND ...   216ms       105us
    @@ 'common' AND ... 21.3s       320ms

An index seek is now a leaf operator. A Doc.title index holds only Doc nodes, so
the index is already label-scoped and seeking it does the label scan's job as
well as its own. That is a property of per-property indexes specifically: the old
single index spanned every node and could not have replaced a scan.

The planner reaches for it through the hook that already chooses a property index
over a label scan, so a full-text predicate now picks the access path the same
way an equality predicate does.

It only applies in conjunctive positions. Under an OR the other branch can admit
documents the index never names, so seeking would silently drop rows. There is a
test asserting that shape plans a label scan, because the reason is not obvious
from reading the planner and someone will eventually try to widen it.

The row filter, which still answers what the planner cannot seek, now remembers
each search for the length of the query. Every row was asking the same index the
same question, which is quadratic in the corpus; the ratio against a scan was
8.4x, 22.2x, then 152.1x as the corpus grew, and is now 2.4x, 2.7x, 2.3x. The
cache assumes a search is stable within one execution, which is what the scanning
operators have always assumed — they search once when they open and reuse it for
every row.

The searching and the seeking share one function for running the searches and
unioning them, so the two cannot come to disagree about what a disjunction means.

Selective queries also stopped growing with the corpus: 65us, 80us, 105us across
five hundred to eight thousand documents, against 3.9ms, 17ms, 72ms before.

docs: document per-property full-text search and the access path

The architecture chapter described the design this release replaced, from its
overview down to its file listing. Four sections cover what is there now: how a
declaration is stored and why it shares the property index catalog, how one set of
trees carries every index and why the prefix is applied by a view rather than
threaded through a dozen key-building sites, how writes keep indexes current and
what recovery has to redo, and why search became an access path.

The query execution chapter documented an operator that no longer exists and
claimed the planner read indexes rather than scanning all nodes. The second half
of that only became true with this release, so it now says which query shapes it
holds for and which it does not.

Users get the part they can act on: `@@` reads the index when it is the whole
WHERE or a branch of an AND, and examines every node with the label when it sits
under an OR beside a non-text condition. That is a two-hundred-fold difference on
a large label and it is decided by how the query is written, so it belongs in the
guide rather than only in the architecture notes.
